newsitem.title: RUSSIA: ICE HOCKEY-RUSSIAN CHAMPS TORPEDO FACE EURO BATTLE.
newsitem.headline: ICE HOCKEY-RUSSIAN CHAMPS TORPEDO FACE EURO BATTLE.

text.p: Torpedo Yaroslavl, who this week became only the second team from outside Moscow to win the Russian hockey title, face a new battle with the capital over hosting European ties at home next year.

Kimmo Leinonen, an official of the Euroleague tournament which Torpedo should play in next season, told Sport-Express newspaper on Friday that Torpedo would probably have to play in one of the bigger arenas of Moscow or St Petersburg if they wanted to host foreign opposition.
For the first time in the 50-year history of Soviet and Russian hockey no Moscow club finished in the top three.

The Yaroslavl rink, 260 km (170 miles) north of Moscow, seats only 4,200 -- 800 short of the Euroleague's minimum. The city of half a million also lacks an international airport and has relatively little modern hotel space.
Torpedo stunned Russian hockey when they completed a playoff sweep with a 3-0 final series victory over reigning champions Lada Togliatti on Wednesday.
The third seeds took both games on home ice over the weekend then beat Lada, the only other previous non-Moscow title-winners, 4-1 in Togliatti to claim their first crown.

It was the first year the championship, renamed the Russian Hockey League, had cut out clubs from other former Soviet republics -- a move intended to improve quality and cut travel costs for cash-strapped teams.

The historic win under Pyotr Vorobyev, coaching just his first season at Yaroslavl, earned Torpedo the right to a Euroleague spot alongside European cupholders Lada and Dynamo Moscow, who clinched their place on last season's performance.

The success of Torpedo and Lada, who became the first Russian team to win a major international title since 1993 when they claimed the European Cup in December, underlines the continuing decline of the once powerful Moscow teams.
Besides Torpedo and Lada, provincial teams like Tyumen, Magnitogorsk and Kazan continued their climb, an indication of a new effervescence in Russian hockey.
Regional politicians and businesses pumping money into the sport are helping to reverse the years of decline that followed the collapse of the Soviet sporting empire.

Yet a reminder that the big money, and Russia's biggest hockey stars, are still on the other side of the hemisphere, in the NHL, is that it is likely that neither of this year's finalists will provide players for the national squad at the world championships in Finland this month.
